newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU Commission tries to reassure left-out easterners.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission tries to reassure left-out easterners.

text.p: The European Commission tried to reassure five rejected eastern European countries on Wednesday they were not being left out of the European Union's grand plan to expand into the east.

And as another five countries -- Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Estonia and Slovenia -- basked in the euphoria of being judged ready to start EU entry talks, the executive told them not to rest on their laurels -- membership would not come easy.

Presenting its long-awaited Agenda 2000 policy document mapping out plans to expand the bloc beyond the former Iron Curtain early next century the Commission said Slovakia, Lithuania, Latvia, Romania and Bulgaria were clearly not ready.

"...There is a clear distinction between those applicants whose progress until now creates the reasonable expectation that they will be able to assume the obligations of membership in the medium term...and those for whom such an expectation is not yet justified," External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek told the European Parliament.

Fearful of creating a popular backlash in the countries having the greatest difficulty shaking off their Soviet- dominated past, the Commission was at pains to say the five excluded countries were not being left out in the cold.
"It is not a process of exclusion. On the contrary, it's a process of inclusion that will be pursued permanently," Commission President Jacques Santer told a news conference.

"Differentiation in no sense means discrimination. There will not be ins and outs, but ins and pre-ins with the possibility of the latter to join the former as soon as the conditions are met," Van den Broek told the European Parliament.
The five left out have in a matter of days received a double rejection from the West. On July 8, the NATO military alliance agreed to admit only Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary.
The Commission said it could not let itself be influenced by NATO's decision, but it could do its best to prepare those left out for eventual membership.
Under the Commission plan the five which will not start talks this time will get a special pre-membership status under which their applications will be reviewed each year.

Van den Broek said that while those left out could catch up, the five judged ready for talks should not take early entry for granted and the Commission has earmarked 75 billion Ecus ($82.5 billion) to help all 10 candidates.

"There is no necessary link between the number of countries with which the Union begins negotiations and the number of countries that eventually join the Union in a first wave. Each negotiation is separate and pursues its own course..," he said.

Although none of the applicants was judged ready economically, Van den Broek said the Commission has chosen the five who in the medium term would be ready, without unreasonably long negotiations or transitional periods.
Important work still has to be done economically, including reform of the countries' banking sectors, he said.

At the end of the day EU leaders meeting in Luxembourg in December will have the final say over how many countries are admitted to entry talks and governments are expected to bring all their national interests to bear over the coming months in deciding the size of the EU's first eastwards expansion.
